sections.html:
The city stands on the Potomac's west bank facing Washington, D.C., and measures roughly 15.5 square miles. Arlington County lies north and northwest, and Fairfax County lies south. Its 2020 population was 159,467. Some mailing addresses that say Alexandria actually fall in Fairfax County, so make sure your parcel is inside the city before relying on the rules here.

Two annexations, in 1930 and 1952, each roughly doubled the land area, which is why the western half of the city looks so different from Old Town. House numbering follows that patchwork. In Old Town, numbers run north and south from King Street and west from the river. In Del Ray and St. Elmo they run east and west from Commonwealth Avenue. Out west they run north and south from Duke Street. Buyers, appraisers and title companies all find the neighborhood name as useful as the street address.

Nineteen small area plans guide the city, each covering a different mix of housing. Find yours to get a sense of who will want to buy.

  • Old Town and Old Town North: rowhouses and older detached homes near the waterfront and King Street.
  • Parker Gray and the Braddock Road area: a historic district close to a Metro station.
  • Del Ray and Rosemont: older neighborhoods with a commercial strip on Mount Vernon Avenue in Del Ray.
  • Potomac Yard: newer development on a former rail yard, with its own Metro station.
  • Alexandria West, Beauregard, Seminary Hill and Cameron Station: larger lots, garden apartments and townhouse communities along the I-395 corridor.

Demand follows federal and professional jobs. About 87 percent of people working in Alexandria commute in, so many buyers want a short trip to Metro or the I-395 corridor. Federal moves and contract changes sometimes force owners to sell fast.

Parts of Alexandria flood. The city says about 20 percent of its area was mapped in a FEMA floodplain as of 2011, and heavy storms can flood places outside the mapped zones too.

A city storm sewer study found 83 problem areas across eight watersheds, with Hooff's Run and Four Mile Run each holding 23 of them. The sewers are built to a 10-year storm standard, and the July 23, 2020 storm was about 30 times more intense than that. Hooff's Run carries water from parts of Northridge, Del Ray and Rosemont, so owners there hear about drainage often.

As a Class 6 community in the National Flood Insurance Program's Community Rating System, Alexandria can offer residents a discount of up to 20 percent on flood insurance premiums. A flood mitigation grant program and help with sewer backflow prevention are also available. See the city's flooding and drainage page.

On the state disclosure form the owner makes no claim about special flood hazard areas, and buyers are sent to FEMA maps. Even so, expect questions if your basement ever took in water, and answer in writing.

The Board of Architectural Review controls exterior changes in two local historic districts and on designated buildings that are 100 years old or older. The Old and Historic Alexandria District was the third historic district created in the country, and the Parker Gray District is the second local district.

New construction and exterior changes visible from a public way require the board's Certificate of Appropriateness. A Permit to Demolish is also needed to remove more than 25 square feet of material from a structure, even when it is out of sight from the street.

The sale itself is not restricted, but repairs may be. Anyone planning a renovation will allow for review time, and if you want to fix a roof, swap windows or remove a porch before listing, approval may come first. Preservation staff can be reached at preservation@alexandriava.gov or 703.746.3833, and the preservation page has a tool for checking whether a property is under review. Zoning text changes affecting the districts and the 100-year-old building list have been under discussion, so confirm current rules with staff.

Owners of a worn house in a district often pick an as-is cash sale, since the buyer deals with approvals.

Renting a property for stays under 30 consecutive days on more than 10 days in a calendar year requires a Short-Term Residential Rental Permit, issued by the Department of Planning and Zoning. Council adopted the rules on March 15, 2025, and the department took over administration in September 2025. Operators must give guests a Good Neighbor Guide at least 24 hours before check-in and install required safety equipment.

If the house hosted guests, collect permit papers or application records before listing. Buyers want to know if the permit transfers or must be restarted, and only the city can say. Contact the department through the short-term rental page.

sections.h2: What you owe when the deed is recorded
sections.html:
Sellers owe a state grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of price by default; a contract can hand some or all of it to the buyer. State and locality divide the money equally, and no deed is recorded by the circuit court clerk until it is paid.

Two more state rules matter at closing. Delinquent real estate tax outranks all other liens, which means the settlement agent deducts it from your proceeds. The current year is normally split in the contract. The buyer must also receive the Real Estate Board's residential property disclosure statement, where you make no promises about matters such as historic district rules, flood hazard areas, wastewater systems and radon.

Your settlement agent will quote the recording charges. The statute is posted at Virginia Code 58.1-802.

sections.h2: How a cash sale usually goes
sections.html:
Without a mortgage approval step, a cash purchase can close when you want it to. Describe the house to us, and after a review we send a written offer. Accept it, and a local title company takes care of the deed, the taxes and any loan payoffs.

Before choosing, pull together what the title company will request: loan payoff details, permit or approval records and the disclosure statement. Get a written payoff on every lien and check that the closing date fits your move. Buying as is, we do not ask for a new roof or a fresh coat of paint, and that helps where exterior work needs review.

This page offers general information only, not the advice of a real estate attorney or tax professional.

faqs.q: Do I need city approval to sell a house in an Alexandria historic district?
faqs.a: Not to sell. Exterior work, new construction and demolition of over 25 square feet do need Board of Architectural Review approval, so check with preservation staff before repairs.

faqs.q: How much is the Alexandria short-term rental permit?
faqs.a: $350 a year when the owner does not live there, $100 a year when the owner does. It applies to stays under 30 days on more than 10 days in a year.
In some places, yes. As of 2011 roughly 20 percent of the city sat in a mapped FEMA floodplain, and hard storms have flooded streets beyond it. Hooff's Run and Four Mile Run are known trouble spots.

faqs.q: Who pays the Virginia grantor's tax when I sell?
faqs.a: The seller, by default, at 50 cents per $500 of price. A contract can move part or all to the buyer, and the settlement agent can give you the exact amount.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Alexandria house as-is if it needs major repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. The state form expects buyers to inspect, and selling as is for cash is common when repairs loom. The disclosure statement still goes to the buyer.
